title: When the job disappears, not the person
subtitle: Redundancy: definition, fair selection and collective consultation
objectives: State the statutory definition of redundancy in s 139 ERA 1996, including the diminished-requirement limb and the closure limb

Explain what makes a redundancy selection process fair — a properly defined pool and objective, consistently applied criteria — and how the s 188 TULRCA 1992 collective consultation duty differs from individual consultation
Apply the redundancy definition and the collective consultation duty to new fact patterns, and identify when a protective award is available

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory definition of redundancy: business closure, workplace closure, or a diminished requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind

leadingAuthorities.citation: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, s 188
leadingAuthorities.role: The duty to consult appropriate representatives collectively where 20 or more redundancies are proposed at one establishment within 90 days

leadingAuthorities.citation: Murray v Foyle Meats Ltd [1999] UKHL 30
leadingAuthorities.role: The test for whether the requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind has diminished looks at the requirement for the work overall, not the individual employee's own duties

leadingAuthorities.citation: Safeway Stores plc v Burrell [1997] ICR 523
leadingAuthorities.role: The three-stage approach to identifying a redundancy: was the employee dismissed; had the requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind ceased or diminished; was the dismissal caused, wholly or mainly, by that state of affairs

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite 'redundancy means the job's gone, not the person'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You know the slogan — this lesson checks whether you can apply the actual three-stage test underneath it.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions distinguishing genuine redundancy from disguised reorganisation and testing the collective consultation threshold.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the s 139 definition and the *Safeway v Burrell* three-stage test are the foundation everything else in this lesson (selection, consultation, protective awards) builds on.

overview.hook: A company keeps exactly the same total headcount, but moves three warehouse roles into a single 'multi-skilled operative' position and dismisses the three post-holders who don't get it. Is that redundancy? Most students' gut answer is no — nobody left, nothing closed. The statute disagrees, and the reasoning behind that disagreement is the whole of this lesson.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The redundancy definition, selection principles and collective consultation duty covered here are long-settled law and not subject to any pending reform; they sit apart from the Employment Rights Act 2025 changes covered elsewhere in this module.

parts.heading: What redundancy actually means in law
parts.voice: argumentative — corrects a common misconception before building the real test
body: Ask most people what 'redundancy' means and you'll get something like 'the company doesn't need as many people'. That's close, but it's not what s 139 ERA 1996 actually says — and the gap between the two matters enormously in practice, because employers sometimes dismiss under the banner of 'redundancy' when the statutory definition isn't actually satisfied, which converts what looks like a routine process into an ordinary — and potentially unfair — dismissal.

Section 139(1) sets out two routes into redundancy. The first is closure: the employer has ceased, or intends to cease, carrying on the business altogether, or carrying it on at the place where the employee was employed. The second, and by far the more litigated, is a diminished requirement: the requirements of the business for employees to carry out work of a particular kind have ceased or diminished, or are expected to.

Notice what the diminished-requirement limb does not say. It doesn't ask whether this particular employee's job title has vanished, or whether the total headcount has fallen. It asks whether the business's requirement for a particular kind of work has gone down — which is exactly why reorganisations that redistribute the same overall workload across fewer, differently-defined roles can still be redundancies, even with no change in total staff numbers.

components.definition: A dismissal caused by business or workplace closure, or by a diminished requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind — assessed by looking at the business's need for that kind of work overall, not at whether any one individual's specific duties have disappeared.

interaction.prompt: A business keeps its total headcount unchanged but reorganises three specialist roles into one broader role, dismissing the three specialists who don't get the new role. Can this still be a redundancy under s 139?
options: Yes — the requirement for employees to do the particular kind of work the specialists did has diminished, even though total headcount is unchanged
No — redundancy requires the total number of staff to fall
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Section 139 asks whether the requirement for a particular kind of work has diminished, not whether headcount overall has dropped — a reorganisation that eliminates a category of role can be redundancy even at constant headcount.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — headcount falling isn't the test. Look again at what the diminished-requirement limb of s 139 actually asks: whether the business's need for a particular kind of work has gone down, which a reorganisation can achieve without cutting total staff at all.

parts.heading: The three-stage test, and where selection fairness fits
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the lesson assumes
body: *Safeway Stores plc v Burrell* [1997] ICR 523 turned s 139 into a workable three-stage question that tribunals still use: was the employee dismissed; had the requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind ceased or diminished (or was it expected to); and was the dismissal caused, wholly or mainly, by that state of affairs? *Murray v Foyle Meats* [1999] UKHL 30 confirmed the second stage looks at the business's overall need for the kind of work, not at the individual claimant's own precise duties — an employer cannot escape a genuine redundancy situation by arguing a particular employee's day-to-day tasks hadn't literally disappeared.

Establishing that a genuine redundancy situation exists is only the first hurdle. The dismissal must also be fair in the way it was carried out — which turns on two further questions: was the pool of employees considered for selection a reasonable one, and were the selection criteria applied to that pool objective and consistently applied? An employer who defines the pool so narrowly that it captures only the employee they want to remove — say, a pool of one, drawn around a single unpopular employee rather than the group genuinely doing interchangeable work — risks the whole process being found unfair, whatever the underlying business rationale for reducing headcount.

Selection criteria themselves should be capable of objective assessment — skills, qualifications, attendance and disciplinary records, standard of work — rather than vague, unmeasurable judgments that invite a tribunal to suspect the outcome was decided first and the criteria fitted around it afterwards.

components.text: For the purposes of this Act an employee who is dismissed shall be taken to be dismissed by reason of redundancy if the dismissal is wholly or mainly attributable to — (a) the fact that his employer has ceased, or intends to cease, to carry on the business for the purposes of which the employee was employed by him, or to carry on that business in the place where the employee was so employed, or (b) the fact that the requirements of that business for employees to carry out work of a particular kind, or for employees to carry out work of a particular kind in the place where the employee was so employed, have ceased or diminished or are expected to cease or diminish.
elements: Business (or workplace) closure — actual or intended
Diminished requirement for work of a particular kind — actual or expected
The dismissal must be wholly or mainly attributable to one of these

interaction.prompt: Under s 139(1)(b), what exactly must have diminished for a dismissal to be by reason of redundancy?
options: The requirement of the business for employees to carry out work of a particular kind
The specific individual's own personal workload, however the business's overall needs have changed
The company's total profit for the relevant financial year
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — and *Murray v Foyle Meats* confirms this is assessed at the level of the business's requirement for the kind of work, not the individual claimant's precise day-to-day tasks.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at s 139(1)(b)'s wording — it targets the business's requirement for a particular kind of work, not any individual employee's personal workload and not the company's profitability.

parts.heading: When redundancy becomes collective: the s 188 threshold
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Everything so far applies whether an employer is dismissing one employee or a hundred. Once the scale crosses a specific threshold, though, a separate and much more demanding statutory duty is triggered: collective consultation under s 188 TULRCA 1992.

The duty bites where an employer is proposing to dismiss as redundant 20 or more employees at one establishment within a period of 90 days or less. Cross that threshold and the employer must consult 'appropriate representatives' — either recognised trade union representatives or elected employee representatives — about ways of avoiding the dismissals, reducing the numbers to be dismissed, and mitigating the consequences of the dismissals that do go ahead. This is a genuinely different obligation from the individual consultation an employer should carry out with each affected employee about their own selection; both duties can apply side by side.

The consultation must begin 'in good time' and, critically, before any dismissal notices are given — an employer cannot issue notices first and consult afterwards. Minimum consultation periods apply: at least 30 days where 20–99 redundancies are proposed, and at least 45 days where 100 or more are proposed, running before the first dismissal takes effect.

components.label: The s 188 collective consultation duty
points: Triggered by 20+ proposed redundancy dismissals at one establishment within 90 days or less
Consultation must be with 'appropriate representatives' — recognised union reps, or elected employee reps if none
Topics: avoiding the dismissals, reducing the numbers, mitigating the consequences
Must begin before any notice of dismissal is given, and 'in good time'
Minimum period: 30 days (20–99 proposed redundancies); 45 days (100 or more)

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that triggers the s 188 collective consultation duty on these facts.
interaction.scenarioText: A logistics company proposes to make 24 warehouse staff redundant at a single depot, all within a six-week window, due to falling order volumes. Management plans to issue dismissal notices the following week without any prior consultation.
tappableSpans: plans to issue dismissal notices the following week without any prior consultation
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the trigger — 24 proposed redundancies at one establishment clears the 20-employee threshold, and the six-week window is comfortably inside the 90-day period, so the s 188 duty applies regardless of the other facts.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the headline number against the statutory threshold. 20 or more proposed redundancies at one establishment within 90 days triggers s 188 — the plan to skip consultation is what breaches the duty, not what triggers it.

parts.heading: What happens when consultation is skipped
parts.voice: structural — traces the consequence of the duty through to remedy
body: Failing to comply with s 188 doesn't make the individual redundancy dismissals themselves automatically unfair in the way s 99 or s 103A dismissals are — that's a separate question, assessed under the ordinary unfair dismissal framework and the fairness principles from Parts 1–2. What a s 188 breach produces instead is a freestanding remedy: the protective award, under s 189 TULRCA 1992.

An employment tribunal can order a protective award of up to 90 days' actual pay per affected employee where the employer has failed to consult as required. The award isn't automatically fixed at 90 days — the tribunal decides the appropriate period 'as it considers just and equitable', having regard to the seriousness of the employer's default — but 90 days is the statutory ceiling, and a wholesale failure to consult at all tends to attract an award at or near that maximum.

The sequence worth holding in your head: identify a genuine s 139 redundancy situation → check whether the 20-employee/90-day threshold is crossed → if so, confirm collective consultation happened properly and in time → a failure at that last step opens up protective award liability, on top of (not instead of) whatever the individual fairness of each dismissal turns out to be.

components.label: Consequence of a s 188 breach
points: Failure to consult collectively does not itself make the individual redundancy dismissal unfair — that's assessed separately
It instead exposes the employer to a protective award claim under s 189 TULRCA 1992
Maximum: up to 90 days' actual pay per affected employee
The tribunal sets the actual period as 'just and equitable', reflecting how serious the failure was

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a tribunal works through when a large-scale redundancy exercise is challenged.
items: Confirm a genuine s 139 redundancy situation exists
Check whether the 20-employee/90-day collective consultation threshold is crossed
If crossed, assess whether consultation happened properly and in time
If consultation failed, consider a protective award under s 189, separately from the fairness of each individual dismissal
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure — redundancy status, then the collective threshold, then compliance, then remedy. Each stage is a separate question, and getting the order right stops you conflating a protective award claim with an ordinary unfair dismissal claim.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — you need a genuine redundancy situation before anything else matters, then the collective threshold question, then whether consultation actually happened properly, and only then does the protective award question arise.

parts.heading: Genuine redundancy or disguised reorganisation?
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard distinction before resolving it
body: Here's the distinction examiners return to most often: how do you tell a genuine redundancy from a reorganisation dressed up as one — where an employer really just wants to remove a particular individual and reaches for 'redundancy' as convenient cover?

The answer lies back in the *Safeway v Burrell* third stage: was the dismissal caused, wholly or mainly, by the diminished requirement for work of a particular kind? If the underlying work genuinely still needs doing, in substantially the same volume, by someone, then dismissing one employee and immediately recruiting a replacement to do essentially the same job under a different title is strong evidence the 'redundancy' label doesn't fit — whatever the employer calls it. Genuine redundancy requires that the need for that kind of work has actually gone down, not merely that the employer would prefer a different person doing it.

This matters for both remedy routes covered in this lesson: a sham redundancy dismissal can be an ordinary unfair dismissal (the reason given wasn't the real reason, or wasn't a fair reason properly applied), and if it was used to disguise dismissing 20 or more people while dodging consultation, it can also expose the employer to protective award liability for the underlying collective exercise it was really running.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often accept an employer's own label — 'this was a redundancy' — at face value once any restructuring is mentioned in the facts.
components.whyItsWrong: The label doesn't control the legal analysis. The *Safeway v Burrell* third stage requires the dismissal to actually be caused by a genuine diminished requirement for the kind of work — if the same work persists and someone new is doing it shortly afterwards, that causal link is missing, whatever the employer called the process.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to be a genuine redundancy under the s 139/Safeway v Burrell test?
interaction.scenarioA: A regional sales team of eight is reduced to five after a permanent, significant drop in the volume of accounts the business handles in that region, with the surviving five absorbing the reduced workload.
interaction.scenarioB: An employee is dismissed and told her role is 'redundant', but the business advertises for, and fills, an almost identical role under a new job title within a fortnight.
interaction.explanation: A shows a genuine diminished requirement for work of a particular kind — the underlying volume of work has actually dropped. B is the classic warning sign of a disguised, non-genuine redundancy: the work persists and is quickly refilled, suggesting the real reason for dismissal lies elsewhere.

testPool.prompt: Name the two limbs of the statutory definition of redundancy under s 139(1) ERA 1996.
acceptableAnswers: business/workplace closure and diminished requirement for work of a particular kind
testPool.modelAnswer: Business (or workplace) closure, actual or intended, under s 139(1)(a); and a diminished requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind, actual or expected, under s 139(1)(b).

testPool.prompt: Name the number of proposed redundancies, and the time window, that triggers the s 188 TULRCA 1992 collective consultation duty.
acceptableAnswers: 20+ redundancies at one establishment within 90 days or less
testPool.modelAnswer: 20 or more employees proposed for redundancy at one establishment within a period of 90 days or less.

testPool.prompt: Does a breach of the s 188 collective consultation duty, on its own, make an individual employee's redundancy dismissal automatically unfair?
options: No — it instead exposes the employer to a separate claim for a protective award
Yes — any breach of s 188 automatically renders every affected dismissal unfair

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the maximum protective award a tribunal can order under s 189 TULRCA 1992 per affected employee?
options: A fixed statutory sum equal to one week's pay
Up to two years' gross salary
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes confuse the protective award with the basic award's capped-weekly-pay formula from the unfair dismissal remedies lesson. The protective award is a different mechanism entirely, expressed as up to 90 days of the employee's actual pay, set by the tribunal as it considers just and equitable up to that ceiling.

testPool.prompt: Under s 139(1)(b), whose 'requirement' for work of a particular kind is the relevant question — the business's, or the individual employee's own day-to-day duties?
options: The business's overall requirement for that kind of work, as confirmed in Murray v Foyle Meats
The individual employee's own specific duties, regardless of the business's wider needs
Whichever the employer chooses to characterise the dismissal as

testPool.prompt: Put the Safeway v Burrell three-stage test in the order a tribunal applies it.
items: Had the requirement for employees to carry out work of a particular kind ceased or diminished, or was it expected to?
Was the dismissal caused, wholly or mainly, by that state of affairs?

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that an employer can lawfully choose a selection pool of one employee, drawn around the single person they wish to dismiss, and still expect the redundancy to be treated as fair?
sliderLabels: Confident — pool of one is fine
Confident — this risks being found unfair
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — this risks being found unfair
testPool.explanation: A pool defined so narrowly it captures only the employee the employer wants to remove, rather than the group genuinely doing interchangeable work, is a classic way a redundancy process is found unfair, even where a genuine underlying redundancy situation exists.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a business can be genuinely redundant under s 139(1)(b) even while its total headcount stays exactly the same?
sliderLabels: Confident — headcount can stay the same
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — headcount can stay the same
testPool.explanation: The test is whether the requirement for a particular kind of work has diminished, not whether total staff numbers have fallen — a reorganisation eliminating a category of role can be a genuine redundancy at constant headcount.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the ratio of Murray v Foyle Meats.
testPool.passage: The claimants argued their own individual duties had not changed, so no redundancy situation could exist as to them. The House of Lords rejected that framing. The correct question under s 139(1)(b) is whether the requirements of the business for employees to carry out work of a particular kind have diminished, assessed at the level of the business as a whole, not by comparing an individual claimant's tasks before and after the reorganisation.
testPool.ratioSentence: The correct question under s 139(1)(b) is whether the requirements of the business for employees to carry out work of a particular kind have diminished, assessed at the level of the business as a whole, not by comparing an individual claimant's tasks before and after the reorganisation.

testPool.prompt: An employer proposes 15 redundancies at one site and, separately, 12 redundancies at another site of the same company, both within the same 90-day window. Which statement about s 188 is correct?
options: The s 188 duty is assessed 'at one establishment' — 15 at one site does not on its own cross the 20-employee threshold for that establishment, even though the company-wide total is 27
The two sites are automatically aggregated, so the 20-employee threshold is crossed and s 188 applies to both groups together
s 188 never applies to redundancies split across more than one site
testPool.trapExplanation: The 20-employee threshold is assessed at one establishment, not company-wide. Students often add the two sites' numbers together instinctively — but unless a particular site itself reaches 20 within the 90-day window, s 188 is not triggered for that site on these facts alone; each establishment is considered separately.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more clearly triggers the s 188 collective consultation duty?
testPool.scenarioA: A single branch proposes 22 redundancies within an eight-week period due to a permanent fall in customer footfall.
testPool.scenarioB: A single branch proposes 6 redundancies within an eight-week period, and a further 6 redundancies at the same branch four months later, unconnected to the first round.
testPool.explanation: A crosses the 20-employee threshold within the 90-day window at one establishment, triggering s 188. In B, neither round individually reaches 20, and the two rounds are outside a single 90-day window and described as unconnected, so they are not aggregated to trigger the duty.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most strongly suggests this is a disguised, non-genuine redundancy rather than a real one.
testPool.scenarioText: Daniel is told his role as 'Customer Support Officer' is redundant due to falling demand. Six weeks later, the company advertises externally for a 'Customer Experience Officer' with an almost identical job description and the same reporting line, and fills it.
tappableSpans: told his role as 'Customer Support Officer' is redundant
advertises externally for a 'Customer Experience Officer' with an almost identical job description
testPool.correctSpan: advertises externally for a 'Customer Experience Officer' with an almost identical job description
testPool.explanation: Recruiting almost immediately into an essentially identical role undermines the claim that the requirement for that kind of work had genuinely diminished — the third Safeway v Burrell stage (causation by a genuine diminished requirement) looks shaky on these facts.

testPool.prompt: A manufacturer proposes 35 redundancies at one factory within a 60-day period and gives dismissal notices before starting any consultation with employee representatives. Which statement best captures the legal position?
options: The s 188 threshold is crossed (35 within 90 days at one establishment) and consultation must happen before notices are given, so issuing notices first breaches s 188 and exposes the employer to protective award liability
Because the notices were issued, the s 188 duty no longer applies and cannot be breached retrospectively
s 188 only applies where the employer intends to close the business entirely, not for selective redundancies within an ongoing business
testPool.explanation: 35 within 60 days at one establishment clears the 20/90-day threshold. Consultation must begin before dismissal notices are given; issuing notices first is itself the breach, giving rise to protective award exposure under s 189, regardless of the underlying business rationale.

testPool.prompt: A logistics firm proposes to make 28 drivers redundant at a single depot within a 45-day period, citing a permanent contract loss. Management defines the selection pool as only the five drivers who raised a recent grievance about overtime pay, rather than all 28 affected drivers, and begins issuing dismissal notices the same week the proposal is announced, without consulting any employee representatives. Analyse the legal position.
factsToOrder: 28 proposed redundancies at one depot within 45 days
The stated reason is a permanent contract loss
The selection pool is drawn to include only the five grievance-raising drivers
Dismissal notices are issued the same week, with no prior consultation

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes the Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, and writes the Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a genuine redundancy situation exists, whether the s 188 collective consultation duty was triggered and complied with, and whether the selection process is fair.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 139(1)(b) requires a genuine diminished requirement for work of a particular kind, tested via the Safeway v Burrell three stages and Murray v Foyle Meats' business-wide focus. Section 188 TULRCA 1992 requires collective consultation before notices where 20+ redundancies are proposed at one establishment within 90 days; breach gives rise to a protective award under s 189. Separately, fairness requires a properly defined pool and objective selection criteria.
modelAnswer.application: 28 redundancies at one depot within 45 days clears the s 188 threshold twice over on numbers and comfortably within the window; issuing notices the same week with no consultation is a clear breach, exposing the employer to a protective award of up to 90 days' pay per affected employee. The permanent contract loss supports a genuine s 139(1)(b) diminished requirement. But the pool — limited to the five grievance-raising drivers out of 28 affected — looks targeted rather than reasoned, suggesting an unfair selection process independent of the s 188 breach.
modelAnswer.conclusion: There is likely a genuine underlying redundancy situation, but the employer has breached s 188 (protective award exposure) and has adopted an unfairly narrow selection pool, exposing it to unfair dismissal claims from the five drivers selected on that basis.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is accepting an employer's 'redundancy' label at face value, or assuming the s 188 threshold aggregates across separate establishments or unconnected rounds of dismissal. Check the underlying diminished-requirement causation, and check the numbers against a single establishment within a single 90-day window, before accepting either.
